title: Haryana Seizes 7,500 Kg of Suspected Fake Paneer Bound for Delhi Markets
excerpt: Food safety teams raided four unlicensed dairies in Haryana's Nuh district, confiscating thousands of kilos of synthetic paneer laced with vegetable oils, starches and detergent residue before it reached Delhi markets.
body:
• Food safety officials in Haryana's Nuh district raided four unlicensed dairies and confiscated roughly 7,500 kilograms of suspected adulterated paneer bound for wholesale markets in the Delhi NCR.
  • The raids, carried out by the Chief Minister's Flying Squad with food safety officials and police, uncovered stockpiles of low-grade vegetable oils, industrial starches, chemical emulsifiers and detergent residue at the facilities.
  • The seizure is the latest in an escalating national crackdown: FSSAI has launched a nationwide dairy enforcement drive, and one in five food samples tested since 2020 has been found unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.
  • Authorities have sent samples for laboratory testing and warned of prosecutions, licence cancellations and facility closures as festive-season demand approaches.

Food safety authorities in Haryana have seized approximately 7,500 kilograms of suspected adulterated paneer in a coordinated sweep across four unlicensed dairy facilities in Nuh district, cutting off a supply chain that fed synthetic cottage cheese into wholesale markets across the National Capital Region.

The operation was executed by a multi-agency task force led by the Chief Minister's Flying Squad alongside the district Food Safety Department and local police units, according to EDairy News, which first reported the seizure on Monday. Inspectors struck villages in the Punhana and Ferozepur Jhirka subdivisions, where the dairies were operating without statutory licences or basic food-hygiene compliance.

Beyond the thousands of kilograms of finished product waiting for morning dispatch, enforcement teams found what officials described as the building blocks of synthetic paneer: low-grade vegetable oils, industrial starches, chemical emulsifiers and detergent residue. Samples were collected on-site for laboratory analysis to confirm the exact chemical composition, and consignments deemed immediately hazardous to public health were destroyed.

A racket years in the making

The Nuh raids did not come out of nowhere. The district — formerly Mewat, roughly 130 kilometres from Delhi — has been identified repeatedly as the manufacturing hub for the NCR's fake-paneer trade. An undercover investigation by India Today, whose findings circulated widely in recent weeks, traced adulterated paneer supply chains to hidden units in Firozpur Jhirka, where reporters posing as bulk buyers were shown drums of soybean products, milk powder, palm oil, refined oil and powdered additives used to manufacture paneer-like blocks at a fraction of genuine production cost.

The economics explain the persistence of the racket. Producing authentic paneer requires roughly five to six litres of whole milk per kilogram, tying manufacturing costs to farmgate milk prices. By reconstituting low-value milk solids with non-dairy hydrogenated fats and chemical stabilizers, illicit operators can undercut organised dairy processors by more than half, then sell into price-sensitive urban catering, restaurant and street-food networks where the product is difficult for ordinary consumers to distinguish from the real thing.

Only days earlier, the neighbouring state of Telangana banned artificial non-dairy paneer for one year following its own raids — a signal that the adulteration problem spans multiple states.

Part of India's largest food safety push

The Nuh seizure lands inside what Reuters has described as India's most aggressive food safety enforcement campaign on record. Since 2020, food inspectors have tested more than 100,000 samples annually, with roughly one in five found unsafe, substandard or improperly labelled, according to government data. Nearly 8,000 food business licences have been cancelled in the last three years.

"In a country of 1.4 billion people consuming nearly 1.5 trillion meals every year, ensuring food safety is a monumental task."

— Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI), via Reuters

The national regulator has moved on multiple fronts. FSSAI has launched a nationwide enforcement drive aimed squarely at the dairy supply chain, directing states and union territories to intensify checks on milk collection centres, processing units, transport vehicles, cold storage, wholesale markets and retail outlets — with paneer singled out for special attention because it is easier to adulterate than many other products. In a widely circulated recent video, FSSAI inspectors raided a facility in northern Uttar Pradesh and seized 1,300 kg of adulterated paneer.

Parallel to the raids, the regulator has proposed a red hexagonal front-of-pack warning label for products high in any two of saturated fat, sugar or salt, a measure that has rattled the country's $100-billion packaged food industry. India's Supreme Court was scheduled to review the proposal on September 10.

Why it matters to the diaspora

For Indians visiting home, the raids are a blunt reminder to be selective about where paneer is bought and eaten. Bulk-supplied synthetic paneer moves through catering kitchens, restaurant supply chains and budget eateries rather than branded retail — the places where visitors often eat on short trips. The episode also sharpens scrutiny for diaspora consumers of Indian packaged foods abroad, where the same warning-label debate is reshaping how nutrition information reaches shoppers.

The health stakes are not abstract. Detergent residue and industrial-grade emulsifiers have no place in food, and repeated consumption of synthetic dairy substitutes poses genuine gastrointestinal and long-term health risks — the reason officials described some of the seized consignments as immediately hazardous.

What's next

Authorities say criminal proceedings, facility sealings and prosecutions under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, will be pursued against facility owners, raw-material aggregators and commercial buyers knowingly trading in synthetic dairy. With festive-season demand approaching — the peak window for paneer consumption — officials have warned that highway checkpoints, cold-storage inspections and surprise plant audits will only intensify across Haryana, Uttar Pradesh and Delhi.

The laboratory results on the seized samples will determine the precise charges. But the pattern is now unmistakable: the fake-paneer trade that once operated in the shadows of the Mewat supply chain is being met, finally, with the enforcement weight it always warranted.
image_caption: Cubes of white paneer on a wooden cutting board. Food safety officials in Haryana’s Nuh district have seized about 7,500 kg of suspected adulterated paneer from four unlicensed dairies, part of India’s widening crackdown on synthetic dairy.
nri_angle: NRI visitors should be cautious about paneer served through bulk catering and restaurant supply chains in the Delhi NCR, where synthetic product from illicit dairies has been circulating; the broader FSSAI warning-label push also matters to diaspora shoppers of Indian packaged foods abroad.
author: Diaspora Desk
